title: A Look Back at SDS, Michael Harrington and the Decline of Marxism
author: Kathy Deacon
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Chemnitz_karl_marx_monument-680x540.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/21/a-look-
back-at-sds-michael-harrington-and-the-decline-of-marxism/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Chemnitz_karl_marx_monument-680x540.jpg)

Photograph Source: Velvet - [CC BY-SA
4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)

**(I.) SDS**

According to a familiar narrative, protest is a kind of parlor game of
privileged students. When it occurs on Ivy League campuses, it gets its fair
share of attention, creating an impression that social/political movements
based on long tradition have their point of origin there. (The 170 students
arrested at the City College of New York’s Gaza encampment on April 30, 2024,
largely people of color, had a median family income less than a quarter of
that of the students arrested at Columbia. The news coverage—of their pepper
spraying—and reported tasering—and broken teeth and bones—was delayed a few
days and then relegated to the back pages. (See Sarah Baum in the _Progressive
Magazine_)

In _Campus Wars_ , Kenneth J. Heineman points out that student mobilization
against the Vietnam War-and in support of free speech and the right to
organize on campus-arose initially at publicly funded state universities.

Enmeshed in a hot war and a cold war, awash in DoD grants for war-related
research, the universities assumed a division of labor: Elite schools turned
out foreign policy “experts”; while state schools supplied teachers and
engineers for the home front as well as international policing experts needed
to shore up the unpopular South Vietnamese government.

At Penn State (and Kent State) the “cultural environment was conventional as
well as hostile to dissent.” The antiwar movement “remained small, isolated,
and under ideological and often physical attack throughout the ‘60s.”
(Heineman, p. 270)When General Maxwell Taylor spoke at Penn State in the fall
of 1965, around 30 members of the campus group SENSE peacefully demonstrated
as “prowar partisans marched in an ever-narrowing circle” around them,
“lobbing eggs and hurling obscenities . . . while campus police officers
looked on, prepared to arrest the antiwar demonstrators if they attempted to
break out of the circle.” (_ibid_., p. 150)

“James Creegan [a SENSE partisan], a member of the Penn State Socialist Club
in 1965 and a founder of the campus SDS chapter in 1966, experienced ‘culture
shock’ upon leaving Philadelphia for State College,” Heineman writes. “The son
of an Irish Catholic labor and Communist organizer in Great Britain, who later
immigrated to America, Creegan was frequently assaulted on the campus and in
his dormitory by athletes.”

“Creegan . . . did not believe that the war was a product of American foreign
policy makers’ mistaken reasoning. Rather, the war provided evidence of
American capitalist plans to ‘maintain the entire underdeveloped world as a
source of colonial exploitation . . .

“In October [1965], four members of the Socialist Club and SENSE burned their
draft registration cards at the campus mall as one hundred students watched.
Lively discussion ensued when Creegan urged the student body to ‘join us
against the war machine of United States imperialism which is perpetuating
most of the crimes of this war.’ Hawkish students pummeled Creegan and FBI
agents from Philadelphia soon descended upon State College in search of the
draft resisters.” (_ibid_., p. 149)

As Kirkpatrick Sale points out in his lively, widely regarded as
definitive—certainly indispensable-history of SDS, in those days “imperialism”
and “monopoly capitalism”—necessary concepts—were “out-of-bounds” terms. SDS
would“describe imperialism without giving it that name . . . (Sale, _SDS_ , p.
245)  SDS’s parent/sponsor organization, the (Cold War liberal) League for
Industrial Democracy (LID), funded in part by the AFL-CIO and the
International Ladies Garment Workers Union-both fiercely anticommunist unions-
was irate when SDS in its Port Huron statement (drawn up at its founding
conference in 1962) questioned the motives behind the Cold War. “American
foreign policy in the fifties,” its student authors wrote, “was motivated by a
concern for foreign investment . . . We participated unilaterally–usually
through the Central Intelligence Agency—in revolutions against governments in
Laos, Guatemala, Cuba, Egypt, Iran . . . “

Michael Harrington, the 34-year-old celebrity Socialist author of the best-
seller _The Other America_ , acting as the LID’s liaison with the students at
Port Huron, demanded they deny observer status at the conference to a member
of a Communist party youth group. SDS made it plain they would resist
censorship. So the LID immediately changed the locks on the door of SDS’s New
York office.

(Norman Thomas [the Socialist Party’s _eminence grise_ and six-time
presidential candidate] was then advising young people to go into SDS rather
than his own Socialist Party youth group, the Young People’s Socialist League
(YPSL), “so that they would avoid sterile faction fights and find something
‘more native, more healthy.’’[Sale, p.47] Thomas, a longtime member of the
CIA-linked “Vietnam Lobby,” supported Vietnamese dictator Ngo Dinh Diem’s
decision to cancel the 1956 elections called for by the Geneva accords, for
fear that Ho Chi Minh and the Viet Minh might prevail. (See James Creegan’s
September 17, 2017, article in CounterPunch “The Left Wing of the Permissible:
The Politics of Michael Harrington.”)

Before arriving at Penn State, Creegan became involved with the Progressive
Labor Movement (later the Progressive Labor Party). Organized by ex-Communist
Party members who either quit or were expelled for sympathizing with China in
the Sino-Soviet dispute, its student group, the May 2nd Movement, was the
first to proclaim its resistance to the draft in 1964.

“College students could enjoy a ‘2-S’ student deferment. PLP argued that a
principled anti-war position required refusing this class privilege. . . . As
a result, numbers of PLP members were drafted. PLP’s principled position . . .
won widespread respect throughout the movement” and even “the grudging
admiration of [PL’s] rightwing opponents within SDS.” (See articles written as
a series in _Challenge-Desafio_ during the first half of 2007)

Left-wing parties (such as Progressive Labor, the Socialist Workers Party and
the Communist Party), had a few hundred of their members enlist in the
military, to act as organizers. “They are erased, the same way the recent
PBS/Ken Burns series on the war erased G.I. resistance entirely.“ (See Matthew
Rinaldi, “Waging Peace in Vietnam,” Military Law Task Force, 2019) Penn
State’s SENSE president Andy Stapp, who was stationed at Ft. Still, Oklahoma,
became an organizer of the Soldiers Union and was subsequently court-martialed
in 1967. (Heineman, p. 158)

In 1965, PL urged its members to join SDS and nudge it in a left direction.
“PL helped organize chapters on scores of campuses and became part of the
leadership in many. As the movement grew, hundreds of students joined PL to
‘fight for revolution,’ not just against this particular war.” (_Challenge-
Desafio_)

As the writer Jim O’Brien observed in the November 1977-February 1978 issue of
_Radical America_

> Within SDS, despite the generally unobtrusive nature of PL’s work at first,
> the party came under increasing attack. . . . The attacks sprang in part
> from visceral worry about any disciplined cadre organization working within
> the unstructured milieu of SDS, and in part from PL’s ‘culturally
> retrograde’ opposition to the New Left’s attempts to fuse youth culture . .
> . and radical politics. . . . It had ready answers during a time when SDS
> national leaders were turning to one after another strategy in a series of
> efforts to comprehend the mushrooming student revolt and to decide where
> they should try to nudge it.

After President Johnson escalated the Vietnam War in late 1964 following his
landslide victory in the presidential election, SDS remained “reluctant to pay
attention to any single issue.” But just six weeks later, LBJ launched all-out
war and enlarged draft calls, and SDS, roused to action-energetically rallied
antiwar groups and left organizations; liberal unions like District 65 and
1199; Bronx reform Democrats; and others to a massive April peace march in
Washington, D.C.; 25,000 protestors descended on the nation’s capital, for
what turned out to be the largest peace demonstration in US history. (Sale,
pps.169-76)

However, because Communist groups were invited to participate, the LID did its
utmost to sabotage the march. LID leaders Bayard Rustin, A.J. Muste, and
Norman Thomas—"reluctant to oppose a war that was anticommunist in
intent”-persuaded the _New York Post_ [when still liberal] to run an editorial
featuring their statement opposing the march. Michael Harrington, who did not
sign the statement, raised no objection. He and fellow LID leaders Bayard
Rustin, and Irving Howe remained firmly attached to the politics of the
International Ladies Garment Workers Union (ILG), which, “representing the
liberal wing of the Establishment,” voted at its May convention to endorse
Johnson’s actions in Vietnam and in the Dominican Republic. (Sale, p. 239n)

Although this contributed to SDS’s final rupture with the LID in October 1965,
SDS had yet to develop an antidraft program, or even an official position on
the war itself. To dissociate itself from the ‘draft dodgers,’” its National
Office adopted a “Build not Burn” strategy proposing that alternate service be
made grounds for exemption from the draft. However, the “Boy Scout cast of the
statement”; the fact that it did not attack the draft itself as an inequitable
and undemocratic institution”; did not urge evasion of the draft; or “make any
of the necessary connections between the draft and the war, showing them both
as inevitable products of the American military-industrial state . . . The
apologetic effect of it, especially, irritated many as being too defensive,
too craven . . .”

PL, on the other hand, had adopted a strategy of “Anti-Draft Unions” to
demonstrate at induction centers; oppose college administrations’ cooperation
with the draft; call for no ROTC, military recruitment, or war research on
campus;“Go to High Schools with leaflets, street meetings, . . . union
meetings, etc. . . .” –to bring as many people as possible—particularly
working-class people—into the anti-war movement. (Sale, pps. 232-6)

At this point, SDS’s old guard (seen by many as an elite remote from the rank
and file [_ibid_., p. 248]) were graduating from college and being replaced,
in Sale’s words, by a

> new breed of activist, a younger cohort who, brought to SDS a new style and
> a new heritage . . . For the first time at a meeting people smoked marijuana
> . . . Men grew Pancho Villa mustaches . . .Blue workshirts, denim jackets,
> and boots were worn by both men and women. . . . These were generally people
> raised outside the East Coast, many from the Midwest and Southwest . .
> .often without any family tradition of political involvement, much less
> radicalism. . . .
>
> Not that they were all simply ‘anti-intellectual’, the phrase with which
> many of the old guard and more of the Old Left dismissed them; rather, they
> were generally without exposure to this kind of learning, being
> underclassmen from mediocre colleges or conservative state universities;
> they were nervous and often inarticulate in public debates with well-versed
> old-guard radicals, and they emphasized morals and values, action and
> bodies-on-the-line, honesty and courage, not ideology and theory and what
> they called ‘old Leftism’ and ‘all that thirties horseshit’ . . .

As people still in their teens, five, six, and seven years younger” they were
quicker than the old guard had been “to write off labor, liberals, the
Democratic Party, reforms and the ‘system’ in general . . . “ (_ibid_.
pps.204-6)

In the spring of 1966, President Johnson decided to draft students, and anti-
draft protest and protest against the ranking system began in earnest. FBI
agents approached college deans for SDS membership lists; army intelligence
began sending its agents to campuses. (_ibid_., pps. 262-4)

At televised hearings on the Vietnam war, Arkansas Senator William Fulbright
stated the US _was_ deliberately dropping napalm bombs on South Vietnamese
villages. Although a steady drumbeat of articles and editorials from the NYT
maintained that napalm burns in Vietnam were “negligible,“ through other
sources the truth came to light. The writer Martha Gelhorn managed to convince
the editors of the _Ladies Home Journal_ to run her article about the chemical
effects of napalm, describing through eyewitness testimony how Dow Chemical’s
napalm bombs explode on contact and “melt the flesh.” William Pepper reported
in _Ramparts_ magazine that an estimated quarter-million South Vietnamese
children had so far been killed and another 750,000 wounded. (See Christian G
Appy, _American Reckoning: The Vietnam War and Our National Identity_ , p. 53)

SDS moved from protest to a program of active draft resistance and many young
men burned their draft cards.

In the spring of 1967, PL angered much of the peace movement, and lost much of
its base of support, when it attacked the North Vietnamese for accepting a
small amount of aid from the Soviet Union. PL accused the USSR [seekingdétente
with the West] of colluding with the US to crush the revolution in Vietnam; PL
claimed Moscow influenced the Hanoi leadership to narrow its goals to
independence and national liberation, and retreat from its original position
that there was nothing to negotiate about until the US invaders got out.

Sale claims it was at this point that PL—in a search for new recruits-
developed the idea of a “worker-student alliance” to support striking workers
and the demands of campus workers, and involve workers in antiwar actions-a
strategy they would stick with in the coming years. (_ibid_., p. 332-3) By
contrast, many non-PL SDSers argued that the traditional working class had
become obsolete, was reactionary, and that hope for revolution lay in a “new
working class” of alienated intellectuals and professionals that “lies at the
very hub of production.”

As the Spring Mobilization Committee to End the War in Vietnam held massive
demonstrations on the streets of New York and San Francisco on April 15,
1967-drawing 300,000 protestors (Martin Luther King spoke, appealing to the
Administration to “save our national honor”)-many in SDS were convinced of the
futility of peaceful marches.

> Now for the first time the people around SDS began toying with the idea of
> revolution,” Sale writes. “[A]t this stage something different and . . .
> more comprehensive was wanted, some unified way of talking about the war,
> the military machine, imperialism, complicity, university governance,
> corporate liberalism, and the ‘postscarcity economy. (Sale, pps. 334-7)

At its 1967 summer convention, SDS took an official stand on the war,
repudiating the calls of liberals like Bobby Kennedy for negotiations and a
stop to the bombing; calling instead for immediate withdrawal and an end to
conscription in any form—and went on record in favor of desertion from the
military. (_ibid_., pps. 363-5) As the universities’ role in the war effort
came to light, “an increasing number of sit-ins changed from symbolic acts of
moral witness-where students went limp and were carted off to jail—to
“Tactical Political Resistance”-purposeful obstruction and disruption of
operations such as Dow Chemical recruiting “BY WHATEVER MEANS NECESSARY.”
(_ibid_., pps. 379-382)

On October 21, one hundred thousand people had assembled for a march on the
Pentagon (called by the National Mobilization Committee), when

> . . . suddenly a group of young people—an SDS contingent and some New York
> Yippies—made a breakthrough in the line of soldiers, swept over the weather
> fences, ran past more startled troops, and presented themselves directly to
> the walls of the Pentagon itself. . . .they were beaten with rifle butts,
> hauled away and arrested. By then, however, several thousand more had come
> up behind them; troops and marshals flailed desperately at the crowd, fired
> teargas, used their clubs . . . (Sale, pps. 383-89)

SDS’s National Office, “now began to see itself as the core of a political
revolutionary vanguard. . . . “” _(ibid_., pps.391-2) “Within SDS, the
encounter with Marxist ideas was accelerated by the entry of Progressive
Labor.” (Max Ebaum, _Revolution in the Air, Sixties Radicals turn to Lenin,
Mao, and Che_ , pps. 69-70) PL “persistently invoked ‘the Marxist standards’ .
. . gradually quotations from Marx, then Lenin, and then the modern European
Marxists found their way into SDS and other Movement literature.” (Sale, p.
391)

While rejecting Soviet-style “Communism, SDS leaders disputed the widespread
assumption the October Revolution (which they embraced) led inevitably to
Stalin. As Creegan put it, the Bolshevik party (“in which Lenin by no means
always had the last word”) called for “all power to the soviets”
(democratically elected councils of soldiers, peasants, and workers) at the
moment when Russian soldiers themselves began deserting the Eastern front in
droves, peasants were seizing land from the landlords, and workers were taking
over the factories—actions violently opposed by the provisional government of
Alexander Kerensky, committed as it was to remaining in the war.

SDS leaders viewed the disciplined (“Leninist”) cadre party structure
(operating in secrecy) as more applicable to their situation than the media-
driven “open” political groups they had worked with in the past, such as the
LID or the Democratic party-top-down organizations that no one could
reasonably call democratic. The feeling of necessity for such a cadre party
may have been induced by the fact that the DoD

> recorded (and made available to state and local agencies) the names,
> pictures, locations, and political beliefs of upwards of eighteen thousand
> citizens . . . The Selective Service System issued a directive to local
> draft boards that students involved in draft resistance [or even just SDS
> members in some cases] were to be immediately reclassified 1-A and, if
> possible, packed off to Vietnam.

The FBI openly visited students and faculty and successfully enlisted
administration officials to spy on and submit reports about campus radicals.
Police departments “encouraged right-minded students to report on their
fellows . . . at Penn State a student government rep estimated . . . there
were no fewer than 200 student informants . . . some doing their own private
wiretapping. (_ibid_., p. 406-7)

The Selective Service System was now calling up less than 20 percent of the
college population, “depending for most of its fodder on strata of the society
that were less inclined to make a fuss about it. . . .draft-card burning in
working communities was regarded as faintly cowardly and decidedly unpatriotic
. . .” (_ibid_., p. 422) Police showed little restraint in attacking unarmed
students—the government, university, press, and public supported them.

In response, there grew among some “a willingness to commit violence. Not
violence against people” but “against property . . . connected with a hated or
complicit institution.” SDS did not endorse this position, calling its
perpetrators “the left adventurers” and the “crazies.” (_ibid_., p. 426-8)
While SDS’s national leadership saw the present task as one of “regular
sustained resistance,” PL argued against most confrontations, “avoiding
student power issues which might strike the working class as elitist.”
(_ibid_., p. 397)

During the monthlong strike at Columbia University, 200 students were injured,
another 700 arrested as police violently cracked down on student occupiers. PL
wanted to take the battle off campus and involve people squeezed by Columbia’s
landlordism. (_ibid_ , p. 429-38) The university planned to build a gymnasium
in Harlem, where it owned hundreds of vacant apartments it preferred to keep
vacant rather than rent to residents of Harlem. Advocates of “The New Working
Class” among Columbia’s SDS leadership instead seized upon the strike as “an
opportunity to hold ‘liberation classes’ and reinvent Columbia as a
progressive institution.” [_Challenge-DeSafio_ , spring 2007])

President Johnson called the protestors “young totalitarians.” Congress passed
bills to withdraw aid from ‘disruptive” students,’ . . . and allow the
President to send federal troops, specifically exempted from sanctions on
interfering with an individual’s civil rights, anywhere in the county at his
own whim . . . ” (Sale, pps. 442-6)

> The media, with a predictable measure of exaggeration and paranoia, began
> treating the New Left as if it were a developed and dangerous revolutionary
> threat already, the effect of which was to convince many young people that
> they really were that . . . [C]elebrations of youth culture . . . and the
> embracement of it by wide segments of the capitalist economy, also served to
> convince many that youth had significant power within America and that its
> expression in political terms might be as devastating as its expression in
> cultural ones.. (_ibid_., p.459)

As SDS membership surged nationally, there was a “pervading sense” among some
600 attendees at its 1968 summer convention in East Lansing, Michigan, that
SDS was “the likely organization to be the cutting edge of the second American
revolution . . . ”

Open warfare erupted between PL and the other factions, who elected Bernadette
Dohrn as their Interorganizational Secretary and sought to build an anti-
imperialist youth movement. PL ridiculed them for trying to organize without
the working class. Traditional SDSers labeled PL “external cadre” denouncing
their rigidity, cadre discipline, short hair, and anti-Hanoi politics—Shouts
of “PL out! PL out!” went on for 20 minutes. (_ibid_ , pps. 453-72)

Seeking to deepen the factional crisis, the FBI stepped up its investigation
and penetration of SDS; college administrators opened up their files to the
police and FBI . . .at least 1265 arrests were made. Some campuses banned SDS
outright. “These maneuvers” and “this kind of pressure,” Sale writes, had a
“steadily debilitating effect. . . . [I]n practically no instance were
chapters prepared to deal with phone-tapping, daily surveillance, police
infiltration, large-scale arrests . . . ”

The non-PL faction of SDS rallied around a manifesto "Toward a Revolutionary
Youth Movement,” arguing the route to building a working-class movement lay
through organizing working-class youth. (PL said the Revolutionary Youth
Movement [RYM] placed too much emphasis on youth culture.) Pinning their hopes
for the overthrow of capitalism on “revolutionary” nationalist struggles, RYM
“gave particular attention to the Black liberation movement.”

PL on the other hand, condemned popular positions identified with “Third World
Marxism” and ‘anti-working-class nationalism,’ assuming the standard Marxist
position that the workers of advanced capitalist countries would be the agents
of revolutionary change. They “singled out the Black Panther Party, Elbaum
writes, for special venom.” ( Elbaum, pps. 64-70) (The Panthers “have no class
outlook,” and the aims of black student groups are “limited to securing a
better deal for themselves,” not “at defeating the system.” [Sale, p. 535])

Fistfights between RYM and PL broke out at meetings. RYM divided into two
tendencies: the Weatherman—“in actual practice,” Elbaum notes, “far more
anarchist than Marxist”; and RYM II, which “took seriously the notion of
immersing itself in the working class.”

“How ironic it all was: at precisely the time of the greatest explosion of the
American left in all of the decade, SDS . . . was gradually but unmistakably
isolating and diminishing itself, losing its student constituency, its women,
. . . failing to connect with the high schools, the soldiers, the workers . .
.” (_Sale_ , p. 528): GI resistance had led to the establishment of
coffeehouses. GI newspapers; campus and church sanctuaries for AWOL and
deserting soldiers, and an increase in army desertions. A third of the
nation’s students were involved in strikes. At San Francisco State College,
students boycotted classes for four and a half months to protest institutional
racism and police brutality. (Sale, pps. 512-19)

Nixon’s Attorney General John Mitchell and Deputy Attorney General Richard
Kleindienst, and Hoover’s FBI geared up

> no fewer than twenty federal agencies . . . to maximum surveillance,
> disruption, and harassment of the New Left, among them the army (with
> political dossiers on at least 18 million civilians), the Civil Service
> Commission (with 15 million names of ‘subversive activity’ suspects), the
> Secret Service (with 50 thousand dossiers), the Department of Health,
> Education and Welfare . . . and even the IRS . . .[T]he House Internal
> Security Committee ([had] an admitted 754,000 cards of ‘subversives’ on
> file). Every good-sized city now had its own Red Squad . . .

Hundreds of blatantly unconstitutional bills were introduced in the Senate and
state legislatures -in one instance (West Virginia) giving police

> a license to kill on campus without legal reprisal. . . .
>
> Police or National Guardsmen were called in on at least 127 campuses . . .
> sometimes for weeks on end, and more than four thousand people were arrested
> in campus protests from January to June. In addition, at least one thousand
> students were expelled or suspended . . . making them instantly eligible for
> the draft and a possible future in Vietnam . . . (’signing a death warrant,’
> as it was called).
>
> SDS, the prime target, was banned outright at half a dozen campuses
> (including Kent State), pro-SDS faculty members were fired. (Sale, pps.
> 543-51)

At SDS’s 1969 summer meeting, Bill Ayers and Bernadette Dohrn drew up a
document for PL’s expulsion, calling it “racist, anticommunist and
reactionary.” PLers started to giggle as Dohrn declared PL no longer part of
SDS. She stormed off the stage.

> Hundreds, perhaps seven hundred in all, followed her, their fists raised,
> chanting a mélange of slogans . . . out into the Chicago night.
>
> RYMII formed a unity slate with the Weatherman.” “ . . . Many of the Old
> Left-style sects, such as the Labor Committees, Internationalist Socialist
> Clubs, and the Spartacists, stayed with PL-SDS . . . Others—Yippie
> collectives, the Panthers, and the Radical Union—stayed with the SDS
> regulars. “Plers were not particularly pleased with the split . . . but at
> the moment it seemed best to put as good a face as possible on the whole
> affair and try to claim legitimacy for their side.” (Sale, p. 575)

“[N]one of the high-powered bulwarks of American industry was aware of the
difference between PL and SDS, and assumed that . . . PL . . .was speaking for
SDS and, moreover, the ‘SDS’ of rioting and subversion which the press had
created. In fact, however, PL had no intention of trying sabotage or
disruption or rioting: Its remnants held WSA summer”work-ins” “to give
students . . . some factory line experience.” And better understand the
problems facing workers (_ibid_., P. 597)

In July, RYMII broke with the Weatherman. Widely regarded in SDS as “a bunch
of adventurist fools” (Sale., p.590), they “farmed out in collectives to
poorer neighborhoods of Chicago, pursuing their “kickass” tactics . .
.violently disrupting classrooms in what they called ‘jailbreaks’ in high
schools and community colleges . . . engaging PLers and others who disagreed
with them in bloody fistfights, coming on with macho toughness.”(_ibid_., p.
601)

Of course the media and politicians conflated them with SDS. But SDS had, in
effect, ceased to exist. “Within a few months most SDSers walked away from all
the organized factions.” (Elbaum, pps. 70-1) RYMII’s core membership would go
on to establish Marxist-Leninist collectives—Maoist in orientation—scrambling
to keep up with the twists and turns of the Chinese Communist Party’s foreign
policy over the next decade (which Max Elbaum covers in his history Revolution
_in the Air: Sixties Radicals Turn to Lenin, Mao, and Che_.)

**(II.) Post-SDS**

Creegan, for his part, graduated and returned to Philadelphia. He said that
reading Isaac Deutscher’s biography of Trotsky changed his life. Embracing the
revolutionary Trotskyism of James P. Cannon, he rejected the “Third camp”
position (equal opposition to the USSR and Western imperialism) represented
for a while by Max Shachtman and James Burnham, who later turned much farther
to the right.

Onetime followers of Trotsky, they broke with him on the occasion of the 1939
Hitler-Stalin pact, when they pronounced the USSR a new form of state-
dominated class society, “bureaucratic collectivism,“ as if, protested
Trotsky, the fact of the October revolution could be so easily reversed by the
twists and turns of Stalin’s foreign policy. Trotsky defined the USSR as a
deformed “workers' state.” He believed the overthrow of capitalism in the
Soviet Union was a gain worth defending, and that world revolution would sweep
aside the Stalinist bureaucracy.

Shachtman and Burnham, at the historical moment of the Hitler-Stalin pact,
chose to reject Marxism as well, replacing Marxist “theory” with an empiricism
categorizing a social or an economic formation purely on the basis of its
superficial characteristics rather than its historical development.

The ultimate forbidden text, _Das Kapital_ , [Marxism] the theory that dares
not speak its name—put forth in three dense volumes (if one sets aside the
_Grundrisse_)-a 19th century theoretical landmark whose substance its
opponents seldom address directly—instead maligning it as a “religion”—not a
“science”—because it’s merely “theory” (take that, Darwin; goodbye, Political
Science )-and invoking any “Marxist” bad actor they can think of—to rule out
any possibility the present economic and social system could evolve beyond
this, its final moment—the end of history.

Machines begetting machines—increasingly interconnected—as if forming one big
machine—its ever-diminishing labor component (source of value) embodied in
ever-cheaper mass-produced commodities with an ever-shrinking ratio of profit-
doomed to obsolescence by its own law of development-plagued by recurrent
crises of overproduction and underconsumption; late-stage capitalism is driven
by a profit motive entirely extraneous and unconnected to the need of humanity
in general to survive.

After completing coursework for a PhD in philosophy at the University of
Colorado, Creegan moved to New York in 1979 to study economics at the New
School for Social Research. The campuses were quiet, the war in Vietnam
rebranded now by the right as a “syndrome” preventing Americans from
intervening militarily in other countries. On the left, social democratic
views steadily gained ground over Marxism. (See Christian Appy’s _American
Reckoning_)

Yet wandering into a corner newsstand in Greenwich Village—and other parts of
the city—you still found, beside established publications of the left on the
rack, those of the old left parties and their myriad offspring-a plethora of
magazines and journals of the new socialist parties and preparty formations-
Stalinist, Trotskyist, Maoist and post-Maoist—all with a shared perspective
that capitalism was to be replaced through the agency of a vanguard party-and
still found their authors (who used pseudonyms) at every demonstration and
left event—eager to dispute and discredit one another. New York City’s leftist
_Guardian_ newspaper tried to hold together the remnants of a fractured post-
Maoist camp with an antiimperialist Third World perspective.

Did there really exist a holdover of Marxist intellectuals who had not yet
made a “strategic” retreat into academia or publishing? A familiar figure at
NYC events, Creegan was a fountain of information in the days before
Wikipedia—a genuine public intellectual. Searching for a political home, he
became an “indentured servant” (as he later put it) in the Spartacist League,
a Trotskyist sect attracting other ‘60s campus veterans; he would later
describe it as a cultish formation centered around the needs of its leader,
James Robertson.

Coworkers at the _Village Voice_ in the ‘80s and '90s will recall the eloquent
and erudite shop steward in classified advertising who, when business got
slow, read the _New York Times_ at his desk instead of wasting time trying to
look busy. For over 20 years, he fended off management’s attempts to fire him.
The _Voice_ always dissociated itself from the city’s “hard” left political
culture-giving a vigorous thumbs-up to post-Marxian cultural criticism and
thumbs down to Marxism itself. The ideological framework in place at the paper
enjoined its letters editor from ever running any letter written by Lenni
Brenner, a leftist historian who—although raised an Orthodox Jew-opposed
Zionism.

Shortly before his own death, Creegan spoke at a memorial for Mike Lardner,
one of the founders of the New York Marxist School. He said,

> These days in Greenwich Village you find only ‘68ers’ and millennials at
> Marxist lectures and events. The generations in between are missing. There
> are never any middle-aged people present . . . Marxism fell into a state of
> near extinction until it was revived maybe in somewhat different form . . .
> Broader horizons of possibility may be opening up.

During the Occupy movement a decade earlier, Creegan had joined a revived
Democratic Socialists of America—the organization Michael Harrington
originally helped found in 1982—trebling in size since the Sanders campaign.

A lifelong Marxist, he rejected the notion of transforming a corporate party
into its diametrical opposite-an independent working-class party. DSA’s
strategy of joining the Democratic Party in hopes of pushing it more than
mildly leftward seemed a gargantuan if not hopeless task. But even within the
parameters of what DSA deemed politically possible, Creegan thought the sort
of opportunism practiced by Harrington could only hinder any momentum toward
the development of an independent anticapitalist movement. He summarized his
argument in a long essay that _Jacobin_ refused to publish. It ran in
CounterPunch ([September 7, 2017](https://www.counterpunch.org/2017/09/07/the-
left-wing-of-the-permissible-the-politics-of-michael-harrington/)):

> Harrington joined the youth arm of Norman Thomas’s Socialist Party in 1953,
> and till the end of the ‘60s, remained loyal to its leader, his mentor Max
> Schachtman. who believed the West was engaged in a “progressive” war against
> Stalinism (even though many decades after Stalin’s death). “Shachtman’s
> belief in Western capitalism as the lesser evil . . .led him to support
> America’s worldwide anti-communist crusade, including the 1962 Bay of Pigs
> invasion of Cuba, and-at first only privately-the Vietnam war. Domestically,
> Shachtman came to see the Democratic Party as the political arena in which
> socialists should work, and within the Democratic Party he viewed the AFL-
> CIO bureaucracy –first in the person of United Auto Workers chief Walter
> Reuther, then in the federation’s president, George Meany—as representing
> the true interests of the American working class.”
>
> The emergence of Vietnam as the defining political issue of the ‘60s
> presented a dilemma for [socialists like Harrington] who pursued a strategy
> of leftward “realignment” of the Democratic Party. . . . Johnson had
> appointed Sargent Shriver to head his . . .War on Poverty, which took
> Harrington into its counsels. But even the minor role Harrington played in
> Johnson’s reform team came at a price . . . Harrington was not among the
> most zealous of cold warriors. But despite definite personal misgivings,
> declining to call for US withdrawal from Vietnam was a price Michael
> Harrington was willing to pay for a seat at the table of power throughout
> the Johnson years. During the mid-to-late 60s, he often referred to Vietnam
> as a ‘tragedy’ . . .

Schactman, who privately voiced to Harrington his preference for an outright
US military victory rather than a negotiated compromise—nevertheless "wanted
to maintain some kind of presence in the antiwar movement, where most of the
action on the left was then taking place.” And so, Harrington “helped Shactman
and others organize a new group called Negotiations Now, which promoted itself
as a responsible, moderate alternative to the irresponsible, radical groups
calling for the immediate withdrawal of US forces from Vietnam.”

Harrington finally called for US withdrawal in 1970-three years after Martin
Luther King did. By this time, nearly half the US public was in favor of
withdrawal. “Differences among Democrats were also mirrored among trade union
officials” as Walter Reuther pulled the UAW of the AFL-CIO; the shift was
facilitated by the fact that the war since 1969 was being waged by Nixon.
“Within the Democratic party and union bureaucracy, [Harrington] could
associate himself with a growing liberal wing thatfavored withdrawal for
pragmatic reasons. A stronger antiwar position had, more than being morally
imperative, become politically respectable.”

The split among Democrats and union chiefs resulted in the breakup of the
Socialist Party—the majority, who continued to support the war, followed
Shachtman and Bayard Rustin into the far-right Social Democrats USA. Those who
supported McGovern went with Harrington into the DSOC, which merged with the
New American Movement in 1982 to form the DSA. “One of the agreed-upon
conditions of the merger . . . was support for the state of Israel.”

Creegan notes Harrington’s continued uncritical support of concessionary
“union chiefs” bearing responsibility for the historic defeats suffered by
labor in the ‘70s and ‘80s, whom Harrington never stopped trying to represent
as progressive.

> “Harrington is today a venerable founding father in the eyes of many on the
> left. . . . DSA displays his image on its web page…
>
> Throughout his life Michael Harrington tirelessly devoted his outsized
> talents to his vision of progressive social change. His method was however
> largely confined to cajoling and persuading those who already wielded power
> in politics and organized labor. His insider methods left little room for
> those who would challenge existing authority from the outside or from below.
> . . . Because American workers have never formed a party of their own,
> socialists of Harrington’s persuasion were never able to participate in
> government. Tethered as they remained to the Democratic Party, they lacked
> the opportunity to carry out welfare-state reforms like the ones European
> social democratic governments enacted in the twenty-five ‘golden years’
> following World II.
